title: Motion of Rigid Body
short_intro: The motion of a rigid body is characterized by fixed distances between any two constituent particles under applied forces and torques. It is analyzed by decomposing the motion into translational motion of the centre of mass and rotational motion about the centre of mass.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Kinematics and dynamics of rotation about a fixed axis, moment of inertia, parallel and perpendicular axes theorems, torque, and conservation of angular momentum.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: General general three-dimensional rigid body motion, Euler's equations of motion, principal moments of inertia, and gyroscope precession.

prerequisites: Centre of mass and mass distribution

concept_notes.heading: Kinematics of Rigid Body Motion
bullets: A rigid body is defined as a system of particles in which the separation distance between every pair of particles remains constant over time.
General motion of a rigid body can be expressed as a superposition of translation of its centre of mass and rotation about an axis passing through the centre of mass (Chasles' theorem).
The velocity of any arbitrary point on the rigid body is given by v = v<sub>cm</sub> + ω × r, where ω is the angular velocity vector.

concept_notes.heading: Moment of Inertia and Radius of Gyration
bullets: Moment of inertia I measures the rotational inertia of a rigid body, defined as I = ∑ m<sub>i</sub> r<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> for discrete systems and I = ∫ r<sup>2</sup> dm for continuous bodies.
The SI unit of moment of inertia is kg m<sup>2</sup>, and its dimensional formula is [M L<sup>2</sup>].
Radius of gyration k is the root-mean-square distance of the mass particles from the axis of rotation, related by I = Mk<sup>2</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Theorems of Moment of Inertia
bullets: Perpendicular Axes Theorem: I<sub>z</sub> = I<sub>x</sub> + I<sub>y</sub>, valid strictly for plane laminar (two-dimensional) bodies where axes x, y, and z are mutually perpendicular and intersect at a common point.

Parallel Axes Theorem: I = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md<sup>2</sup>, where I<sub>cm</sub> is the moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through the centre of mass, and d is the perpendicular separation between the axes.
These theorems allow the computation of moment of inertia for complex geometries without evaluating volume integrals directly.

concept_notes.heading: Rotational Dynamics and Angular Momentum
bullets: The rotational analogue of Newton's second law is τ = Iα, where τ is the net external torque and α is the angular acceleration.
Angular momentum L of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis is given by L = Iω.
In the absence of external torques (τ<sub>ext</sub> = 0), the total angular momentum of the rigid body is conserved (L = constant).

derivations.title: Perpendicular Axes Theorem Derivation
derivations.conditions: Planar lamina lying in the xy-plane
steps: Consider a lamina in the xy-plane. Let a mass element dm be located at coordinates (x, y) from the origin.
The moment of inertia about the z-axis (perpendicular to the plane) is I_z = int (x^2 + y^2) dm.
Expand the integral: I_z = int x^2 dm + int y^2 dm.
Recognize that int y^2 dm is the moment of inertia about the x-axis (I_x) and int x^2 dm is the moment of inertia about the y-axis (I_y).

derivations.title: Parallel Axes Theorem Derivation
derivations.conditions: Any rigid body, relating axis through centre of mass to a parallel axis at distance d
steps: Let I_cm be the moment of inertia about an axis passing through the centre of mass, and I be the moment of inertia about a parallel axis at distance d.
The position of mass element dm relative to the centre of mass axis is r_i, and relative to the new axis is (r_i + d).
Write the moment of inertia: I = int (r_i + d)^2 dm = int r_i^2 dm + d^2 int dm + 2d int r_i dm.
Since the axis passes through the centre of mass, the first moment of mass int r_i dm vanishes by definition. Also int r_i^2 dm = I_cm and int dm = M.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torque versus Angular Acceleration Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear graph of net torque (	au) on the y-axis versus angular acceleration (alpha) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line yields the moment of inertia (I) of the rigid body in accordance with 	au = Ialpha.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested numerically and conceptually to extract moment of inertia from experimental data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kater's Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A reversible compound pendulum plotted with time period versus suspension distance from the centre of mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine the local acceleration due to gravity (g) accurately by making time periods equal about two asymmetrical knife edges.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on compound pendulum time period and centre of oscillation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Angular Velocity versus Time in Deceleration
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An exponentially decaying or linearly decreasing curve of omega against t under constant frictional torque.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Area under the curve represents total angular displacement; slope gives angular deceleration (alpha).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical problems involving rotational kinematics under braking torque.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the moment of inertia of a uniform circular disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m about a tangential axis lying in the plane of the disc.
solution_steps: Find the moment of inertia of the disc about a diameter: I_d =  rac{1}{4} M R^2.
Substitute values: I_d =  rac{1}{4} (2) (0.5)^2 = 0.5 	imes 0.25 = 0.125 kg m^2.
Use the parallel axes theorem to shift the axis from the diameter to the tangent in the plane: I = I_d + M R^2.

solved_numericals.question: A solid sphere of mass 1 kg and radius 0.1 m rolls without slipping on a horizontal surface with a linear velocity of 2 m/s. Calculate its total kinetic energy.
solution_steps: Total kinetic energy of a rolling body is the sum of translational and rotational kinetic energies: K =  rac{1}{2} M v^2 +  rac{1}{2} I omega^2.
For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia about its diameter is I =  rac{2}{5} M R^2.
Substitute omega = v / R into the kinetic energy equation: K =  rac{1}{2} M v^2 +  rac{1}{2} ( rac{2}{5} M R^2) ( rac{v}{R})^2 =  rac{1}{2} M v^2 +  rac{1}{5} M v^2 =  rac{7}{10} M v^2.
Substitute numerical values: K =  rac{7}{10} (1) (2)^2 = 0.7 	imes 4 = 2.8 J.

solved_numericals.question: A uniform rod of length L and mass M is free to rotate in a vertical plane about a smooth horizontal axis passing through one of its ends. If it is released from rest from the horizontal position, find its angular velocity when it reaches the vertical position.
solution_steps: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through its end is I =  rac{1}{3} M L^2.
Loss in potential energy as the centre of mass falls by a vertical distance h = L / 2 is Delta U = M g ( rac{L}{2}).
By conservation of mechanical energy, loss in potential energy equals gain in rotational kinetic energy: M g  rac{L}{2} =  rac{1}{2} I omega^2.
Substitute I =  rac{1}{3} M L^2: M g  rac{L}{2} =  rac{1}{2} ( rac{1}{3} M L^2) omega^2.
Simplify and solve for omega: omega^2 =  rac{3g}{L}, giving omega = sqrt{ rac{3g}{L}}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The body is assumed perfectly rigid, meaning internal deformations under applied forces are negligible.
The parallel and perpendicular axes theorems apply strictly to rigid bodies with time-invariant mass distribution.
Frictional forces during pure rolling are assumed non-dissipative in terms of mechanical energy transfer (no micro-sliding).

common_misconceptions.wrong: The moment of inertia of a body is a universal constant independent of the choice of axis.
common_misconceptions.correct: Moment of inertia depends heavily on the orientation and location of the chosen axis of rotation.
common_misconceptions.why: MOI sums the mass-distance squared product (mr^2); changing the axis alters every particle's distance r.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The perpendicular axes theorem can be applied to any three-dimensional object like a sphere or a cube.
common_misconceptions.correct: The perpendicular axes theorem is valid exclusively for two-dimensional planar laminar bodies.
common_misconceptions.why: The derivation relies on z-coordinates being identically zero across the entire mass distribution (sum z_i^2 dm = 0).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Friction always opposes motion and performs negative work on a rolling body.
common_misconceptions.correct: Static friction acting during pure rolling does zero work because the point of contact is instantaneously at rest.
common_misconceptions.why: Work done is force multiplied by displacement of the point of application, which is zero for rolling without slipping.

quick_revision: Chasles' theorem states that general rigid body motion is a combination of translation of COM and rotation about COM.
Moment of Inertia (General): I = sum m_i r_i^2
Radius of Gyration: k = sqrt{ rac{I}{M}}
